rv.q: Indeed, even if the world of Picnic remains both miles and decades away, Gold and his accomplished cast have discovered how to make this underappreciated play feel like a feast for contemporary audiences.
Inge might be amazed that his bittersweet examination of life's disappointments is here presented as a broader comedy, but director Sam Gold and the seasoned cast members mostly make it work.
It's a pleasure to watch the supposedly supporting cast take ownership of these characters.
But as a snapshot of a time and place that shows the solitude of small-town life for so many people, women especially, Picnic yields gentle rewards.
As it stands, this Picnic is an ad hoc smorgasbord, where not all dishes are guaranteed to palate in perfect harmony.

But helmer Sam Gold fails to make any case at all with this clumsy production for the Roundabout, which reduces Inge’s characters to broad caricatures and finds more comedy than pathos in their lives of quiet desperation.
Director Sam Gold’s rich and satisfying revival for the Roundabout showcases in a production packed with fine performances and detailed design.
All in all, though, the production is theater you can sink your teeth into.
This revival proves that some plays are worth waiting for, and that the right cast can make even familiar material feel fresh and urgent.
The voltage is more palpable in Joshua Logan's 1955 film than it is in this earnestly detailed but sexless revival.

So the play about dashed hopes colliding with awakened desires isn't nearly as electric as it could be, but it's still a vintage trip back to muddled 1950s morality and the poetic hopes that rose up in spite of it.
The challenge mostly eludes this production, directed by Sam Gold and featuring such first-rate actors as Ellen Burstyn and Mare Winningham, in which the village innocence tends toward the overdone.
Some of us age better than others.
Coarse, excessively anxious for laughs, and deficient in the repression rampant in 1950s small-town Kansas, the production strands its 12 actors in several very different plays.
Not much in this very professional production feels like it needs to be said.
